doc.title: Al Vollmer interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, June 8, 2017

title: Character of the band and Clyde Bernhardt's career
summary: Vollmer seeks blues inflection; Clyde Bernhardt played with King Oliver and Jay McShann's band with Charlie Parker, and the band changed when Eddie Durham joined.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: But your band has been more about Ellington than —

Well basically what the band is I don’t tell anybody how to play, but if I hear that they’ve got a blues inflection to their playing well that interests me and also, depending on I mean when I had access to the musicians who had done the recordings that I had collected, so I went after some of them, especially if they had any connection to King Oliver. Clyde had some blues with King Oliver and played with him in the 30s. In fact Clyde Bernhardt is rather interesting because when he was with Jay McShann, later, in the 40s, Charlie Parker was in that band. So Clyde Bernhardt represents almost a microcosm in the history of jazz, having played with King Oliver and Charlie Parker. There’s almost nobody else who has. And the thing is the character of the band changes with the musicians in it. So when Clyde left and Eddie Durham came into the band it was a whole different approach.
